ir-1982.blurb: After recapturing Khorramshahr in May 1982, Iran rejected ceasefire offers and invaded Iraq — but Operation Ramadan (July 1982) failed catastrophically near Basra, blunting Iran's offensive momentum and locking the war into a grinding stalemate that lasted until 1988.

ir-1988.blurb: Following Khomeini's secret 1988 order, thousands of political prisoners were executed across Iran; no perpetrators faced domestic prosecution, and Death Commission members — including Ebrahim Raisi — were later elevated to the country's highest offices.

ir-2006.blurb: The UN Security Council unanimously adopted Resolution 1737 in December 2006, imposing mandatory sanctions on Iran over its refusal to suspend uranium enrichment — triggering a sanctions cascade that continued through 2010 and directly preceded the 2015 JCPOA negotiations.

ir-2018.blurb: Following the US withdrawal from the JCPOA in May 2018 and full reimposition of sanctions in November, Iran's oil exports collapsed, its currency lost the majority of its value, and Iran progressively abandoned the deal's nuclear limits — eventually enriching uranium well beyond permitted levels.

ie-1999.blurb: Ireland joined the eurozone on 1 January 1999, transferring monetary policy to the ECB and locking in interest rates too low for its overheating economy; the resulting cheap-credit environment fuelled a property and credit boom that culminated in a banking crisis and EU/IMF bailout in 2010.

ie-2014.blurb: Mass Right2Water protests forced the Irish government into a sustained retreat: water charges were reduced, then suspended in 2016, and permanently abolished in 2017, while the movement contributed to significant electoral realignment in the 2016 general election.

ie-2015.blurb: In May 2015, Ireland became the first country to legalise same-sex marriage by popular national vote, with 62% of voters approving a constitutional amendment; the first same-sex marriages took place in November 2015, marking a definitive shift from the country's historically conservative, Catholic-dominated social order.

il-1972.blurb: Israel authorized Operation Wrath of God, a covert Mossad campaign that hunted those responsible for the massacre across Europe and the Middle East. The effort's most visible strike was the April 1973 commando raid on Beirut, killing three senior PLO leaders.

il-1980.blurb: On 30 July 1980, Israel's Knesset passed the Jerusalem Law, declaring Jerusalem "complete and united" as the capital of Israel. The UN Security Council condemned the law as null and void via Resolution 478, prompting thirteen countries to relocate their embassies from Jerusalem to Tel Aviv.

il-1981.blurb: Three days later, the UN Security Council unanimously passed Resolution 497 declaring the law null and void; Israel refused to comply, and the Golan Heights remained under Israeli control, with the international community continuing to regard it as occupied Syrian territory.

ci-1990.blurb: Houphouet-Boigny won Ivory Coast's first multiparty presidential election in October 1990, defeating opposition leader Laurent Gbagbo, but the ruling PDCI retained dominant control; Houphouet-Boigny died in 1993, and political instability eventually culminated in a military coup in 1999.

jm-2017.blurb: In September 2017, Prime Minister Andrew Holness's government enacted and deployed Jamaica's Zone of Special Operations legislation, establishing emergency security zones in high-violence neighbourhoods — suspending constitutional protections to combat gang crime — a model that drew sustained human rights criticism and was subsequently expanded as the state's dominant anti-gang tool.

jp-2018.blurb: In December 2018, Japan passed its most significant post-war migration law, creating new visa categories to admit foreign workers in labor-shortage sectors — marking a structural departure from Japan's longstanding "no-immigration" principle, though initial uptake upon the law's April 2019 implementation fell far short of targets.

kz-2008.blurb: Kazakhstan's banking sector buckled under overextended foreign borrowing; the government took majority state control of BTA Bank and Alliance Bank by early 2009, and both subsequently defaulted on their foreign debt.

ke-1962.blurb: The 1962 Lancaster House Conference produced a majimbo (federalist) independence constitution for Kenya, but after Jomo Kenyatta became Prime Minister in 1963 and independence was achieved in December 1963, constitutional amendments rapidly stripped away the regional powers in favor of centralized authority.

ke-2001.blurb: In 2001, Raila Odinga's NDP entered a formal coalition with Moi's ruling KANU party — Kenya's first coalition cabinet — and the two parties merged in early 2002, but the union collapsed when Moi chose Uhuru Kenyatta as successor; Odinga defected to the opposition and backed Mwai Kibaki, who ended KANU's 40-year rule in December 2002.

kg-2020.blurb: Disputed parliamentary elections in October 2020 triggered mass protests that toppled President Jeenbekov; released prisoner Sadyr Japarov seized power, won a snap presidential election in January 2021, and pushed through a new constitution concentrating authority in the presidency.

lb-1974.blurb: The compounding pressures of 1974 — Lebanese military operations against Palestinian armed factions in the south, Israeli retaliatory strikes, and cross-sectarian labor unrest — fed directly into the conditions that ignited the Lebanese Civil War in April 1975, one of the most destructive conflicts in Middle Eastern history.

lr-1984.blurb: Liberia ratified a new constitution in July 1984 under Samuel Doe's military government, dissolving the ruling council and establishing an interim assembly with Doe as president; the constitution took full effect after the disputed 1985 elections, entrenching Doe's rule and setting the stage for the First Liberian Civil War.

ly-1978.blurb: In 1978, Gaddafi enacted Law 4/1978, abolishing private rental and converting tenants into legal occupants overnight while landlords lost their properties to the state; simultaneously, the second volume of the Green Book triggered the seizure of private businesses, dismantling Libya's commercial sector entirely.

ly-1986.blurb: Rather than deterring Gaddafi, the U.S. strikes preceded an escalation of Libyan-sponsored terrorism, most directly the 1988 Lockerbie bombing (Pan Am Flight 103, 270 killed), leading to UN sanctions in 1992 and Libya's deepening international isolation.

mg-1996.blurb: Following President Zafy's impeachment and removal from office, Madagascar held a snap election in late 1996 that returned former authoritarian leader Didier Ratsiraka from exile; he then secured a constitutional referendum in 1998 that significantly expanded presidential powers.

mg-2002.blurb: Ravalomanana consolidated power after Ratsiraka fled to exile in France in July 2002, ending months of blockades and armed confrontations — but Madagascar's economy contracted sharply, with all major sectors disrupted by the crisis.

ml-1985.blurb: Mali invaded Burkina Faso in the five-day "Christmas War" (December 25–30, 1985) over the disputed Agacher Strip, ending in a ceasefire and OAU mediation; the ICJ subsequently split the territory between the two countries in December 1986, with both governments accepting the ruling.

ml-2015.blurb: The Algiers Accords produced an uneasy calm rather than durable peace, as implementation across all major pillars remained deeply incomplete; successive crises — including a 2021 military coup and MINUSMA's 2023 withdrawal — further eroded the accord until Mali's junta formally terminated it in January 2024.

mr-2008.blurb: General Mohamed Ould Abdel Aziz's bloodless August 2008 coup ousted Mauritania's first democratically elected president, drawing AU suspension and Western aid cuts; Abdel Aziz won a contested 2009 presidential election, consolidating his rule until 2019.

mx-2019.blurb: In February 2019, Indigenous land defender Samir Flores Soberanes was shot dead outside his home in Amilcingo, Morelos, one day before a government referendum on the Proyecto Integral Morelos pipeline he had opposed — triggering national outrage, intensified scrutiny of Mexico's consultation processes with Indigenous communities, and the eventual suspension of the Amilcingo pipeline section.

mx-2020.blurb: Mexico's economy contracted 8.5% in 2020 — its worst modern downturn — while the March 2020 mass feminist marches against femicide drove a penal code reform adding criminal penalties for public servants who leak crime-scene images.

ma-1995.blurb: Morocco became a founding member of the World Trade Organization on 1 January 1995, having hosted the Marrakesh Agreement signing the previous April, and subsequently participated in the Barcelona Euro-Mediterranean Conference in November 1995, setting the framework for an EU–Morocco Association Agreement signed in 1996.

ma-2015.blurb: In September 2015, Morocco held its first simultaneous local and regional elections under the 2011 constitutional reforms, with the ruling Islamist PJD sweeping all major cities and winning the most regional seats — consolidating its democratic mandate and setting the stage for its 2016 parliamentary victory.

na-2002.blurb: Namibia enacted the Communal Land Reform Act (No. 5 of 2002), formalizing tenure rights over communal lands managed by traditional authorities — but the rights created could not serve as collateral, leaving rural farmers without access to capital and embedding a tenure structure that continues to shape debates over rural poverty.

ni-1986.blurb: The ICJ ruled against the United States in June 1986 for mining Nicaragua's harbors and backing the Contras, ordering reparations the U.S. refused to pay; months later, the Iran-Contra scandal exposed the Reagan administration's covert, illegal diversion of funds to the Contras, triggering Congressional investigations and prosecutions of senior officials.

kp-1976.blurb: North Korea backed down as the US and South Korea mounted a massive show of force (Operation Paul Bunyan, August 21) to finish the tree-trimming mission; Kim Il-Sung issued a rare expression of "regret" — the first North Korean acknowledgment of responsibility for DMZ violence since the 1953 armistice.

om-1972.blurb: The Battle of Mirbat proved the decisive turning point of the Dhofar War: PFLOAG never regained the strategic initiative, Sultan Qaboos's hold on Oman was secured, and the national development program — building roads, schools, and hospitals from oil revenues — accelerated unimpeded through the 1970s.

om-2013.blurb: In 2013, Sultan Qaboos facilitated secret back-channel talks between U.S. and Iranian officials at his Muscat villa, producing the framework for the November 2013 Joint Plan of Action — the first direct U.S.-Iran diplomatic engagement in decades and the direct precursor to the 2015 JCPOA.

pk-1967.blurb: Bhutto's founding of the Pakistan People's Party in November 1967 catalysed a mass uprising that forced Ayub Khan's resignation in March 1969, and Bhutto's subsequent government undertook sweeping nationalisation of major industries and land reform redistribution — the most significant fiscal restructuring in Pakistan's post-independence history.

pk-1974.blurb: Pakistan's Parliament unanimously passed the Second Amendment on 7 September 1974, constitutionally declaring Ahmadis non-Muslims — institutionalising state-sanctioned religious exclusion and anchoring an Islamist political shift with lasting consequences for minority rights and blasphemy law.

pk-1991.blurb: In January 1991, Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif launched Pakistan's landmark privatization programme, reversing Bhutto-era nationalizations; by its conclusion in 1993 his government had privatized two banks and 68 industrial units, though the centrepiece MCB sale was later found by NAB to have involved serious irregularities.

pk-1995.blurb: A foiled Islamist-military coup attempt in September 1995 and concurrent corruption scandals involving PM Benazir Bhutto and her husband Asif Ali Zardari fatally weakened her government; she was dismissed in 1996 and convicted of corruption in 1999.

pk-1997.blurb: After winning a landslide election in February 1997, Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif passed two constitutional amendments concentrating power in the Prime Minister's hands — but the arrangement collapsed in October 1999 when General Pervez Musharraf launched a military coup that overthrew his government.

pk-2003.blurb: The November 2003 ceasefire along the Line of Control held, enabling the January 2004 Vajpayee–Musharraf Islamabad Declaration and the launch of the India–Pakistan Composite Dialogue, which ran through four rounds before being suspended after the November 2008 Mumbai attacks.

ps-2002.blurb: In spring 2002, Israel launched Operation Defensive Shield, reoccupying West Bank cities and dismantling Palestinian Authority security infrastructure. The operation marked a turning point in the Second Intifada, after which violence declined steadily through 2005, while Israel began construction of the West Bank Separation Barrier.

ps-2005.blurb: Israel completed its unilateral withdrawal from Gaza in September 2005, ending 38 years of direct control, but the disengagement yielded no peace framework; Hamas won Palestinian legislative elections in January 2006 and seized full control of Gaza by June 2007, triggering an Israeli-Egyptian blockade and reshaping the conflict's geography permanently.

pa-2018.blurb: In June 2018, former Panamanian President Ricardo Martinelli was extradited from the United States to face charges of illegal wiretapping and embezzlement, but was ultimately acquitted; he later received a 10-year sentence on separate money laundering charges.

pg-1975.blurb: Papua New Guinea declared independence from Australia on 16 September 1975, with Michael Somare as its first Prime Minister, establishing a Westminster-style parliamentary democracy and joining the United Nations the following month.

pg-2020.blurb: Negotiations between the Marape government and ExxonMobil over the P'nyang gas field collapsed in early 2020 after PNG demanded sharply improved fiscal terms, halting the Papua LNG expansion for years and cementing "Take Back PNG" resource nationalism as the defining economic policy of the Marape era.

ph-2002.blurb: The Balikatan 02-1 operation forced Abu Sayyaf out of Basilan by mid-2002, with Philippine forces killing top ASG commander Abu Sabaya in June; the residual US advisory presence was institutionalized as the Joint Special Operations Task Force – Philippines, cementing a long-term US security footprint in the southern Philippines.

ph-2020.blurb: The Anti-Terrorism Act, combined with the ongoing drug war, drew sustained international condemnation and contributed to the ICC authorizing a formal crimes-against-humanity investigation in September 2021; by early 2025 the ICC Prosecutor had applied for an arrest warrant against Duterte himself.

ru-1957.blurb: Khrushchev defeated the Anti-Party Group's coup attempt in June 1957 by taking the dispute to the Central Committee, then turned on his rescuer: Marshal Zhukov was dismissed as Defence Minister in October 1957, cementing Party supremacy over the Soviet military for the remainder of the Cold War.

rw-1975.blurb: In July 1975, President Habyarimana founded the MRND, transforming Rwanda into a single-party state and consolidating executive, military, and judicial power entirely in his hands.

sn-2004.blurb: In December 2004, the Senegalese government and the MFDC signed a General Peace Agreement in Ziguinchor, the most substantive peace milestone in the decades-long Casamance insurgency; the ceasefire held for roughly 20 months before fighting resumed and the accord ultimately collapsed due to MFDC factionalism.

rs-2003.blurb: Serbia declared its first state of emergency since World War II and launched Operation Sabre, detaining over 11,000 people linked to organised crime; the assassination nonetheless dealt a lasting blow to democratic reform and Euro-Atlantic integration, with trials concluding in 2007 with 40-year sentences for the chief conspirators.

sl-1991.blurb: The RUF's March 1991 invasion triggered an eleven-year civil war that killed tens of thousands and displaced millions; a new multi-party constitution adopted that same year was almost immediately suspended following a military coup in 1992.

sg-1991.blurb: In 1991, Singapore transformed its presidency from an appointed post to a directly elected office with veto powers over national reserves and key appointments — a structural check on the elected government that took effect on 30 November 1991 and produced Singapore's first presidential election in 1993, won by Ong Teng Cheong.

sk-2018.blurb: The murders of journalist Ján Kuciak and his fiancée sparked the largest protests in Slovakia since 1989, driving Prime Minister Robert Fico and his entire cabinet to resign in March 2018.

si-2021.blurb: In the second half of 2021, Slovenia held the Presidency of the Council of the EU, hosting the EU–Western Balkans Summit at Brdo pri Kranju in October; the presidency reaffirmed enlargement conditionality and greenlit Croatia's path to Schengen membership.

za-2018.blurb: Zuma resigned in February 2018 under ANC pressure, and Cyril Ramaphosa was sworn in the following day, signalling a break from the state capture era; though South Africa entered a brief technical recession mid-year, the economy rebounded in Q3 2018.

kr-1979.blurb: Following Park's assassination, General Chun Doo-hwan seized power through an intra-military coup in December 1979, suppressed the Gwangju pro-democracy uprising in May 1980, and assumed the presidency in August 1980, extending authoritarian rule until South Korea's democratic transition in 1987.

kr-1987.blurb: Facing mass protests, the regime accepted direct presidential elections via the June 29 Declaration; a new constitution was ratified by referendum in October 1987, and South Korea held its first direct presidential election in December, ending two decades of military rule and inaugurating the Sixth Republic.

es-1997.blurb: ETA's murder of PP town councillor Miguel Ángel Blanco in July 1997 sparked mass protests across Spain, with over six million people taking to the streets — an outpouring known as the "Spirit of Ermua" that dramatically eroded ETA's public legitimacy and marked the beginning of the group's terminal decline.

sd-1997.blurb: In November 1997, President Clinton signed Executive Order 13067, imposing comprehensive US trade and financial sanctions on Sudan over its support for terrorism and human rights abuses. The sanctions regime lasted roughly 20 years, contributing to severe economic isolation, before being lifted in 2017.

sd-2018.blurb: Mass protests that erupted in December 2018 over bread and fuel price hikes spread across Sudan and sustained for months until, on 11 April 2019, the military arrested President Omar al-Bashir, ending his 30-year rule and transferring power to a transitional military council.

sr-2011.blurb: As the court-martial of President Bouterse for the 1982 December Murders entered its final evidentiary phase in 2011, his party passed an amnesty law in April 2012 that immediately suspended the trial — just as sentencing approached — drawing international condemnation from the UN, Amnesty International, and Human Rights Watch.

se-1973.blurb: The six-day Norrmalmstorg bank siege in Stockholm (August 1973) ended with the surrender of hostage-taker Jan-Erik Olsson and his accomplice Clark Olofsson; the episode gave rise to the globally recognized psychological term "Stockholm syndrome," describing the emotional bonds hostages sometimes form with their captors.

se-1995.blurb: Following a November 1994 referendum in which 52.3% voted in favour, Sweden acceded to the European Union on 1 January 1995 alongside Austria and Finland, ending its Cold War policy of neutrality and integrating it fully into the EU's single market and institutions.

se-2018.blurb: Sweden's September 2018 election produced a hung parliament, triggering 134 days of deadlock before the "January Agreement" installed a minority Social Democrat–Green cabinet (Löfven II, January 2019), propped up by Liberal and Centre Party defections from the fractured centre-right Alliance.

sy-1972.blurb: The Tabqa Dam on the Euphrates — Syria's largest infrastructure project, built with Soviet financing and expertise — was inaugurated in July 1973, creating Lake Assad and transforming Syrian irrigation capacity. It became a defining symbol of Hafez al-Assad's Ba'athist state-building program.

sy-2009.blurb: By 2009, Syria's catastrophic 2006–2010 drought had stripped 800,000 Syrians of their livelihoods and displaced up to 1.5 million rural people to urban slums — a stress multiplier analysts link directly to the outbreak of the 2011 civil war.

sy-2021.blurb: In May 2021, Bashar al-Assad was declared the winner of Syria's presidential election with 95.1% of the vote, securing a fourth term; the result was condemned as illegitimate by the UN, the US, and major European governments, deepening Syria's diplomatic isolation and effectively burying the UN-backed Geneva peace process.

th-1984.blurb: In 1984, Thailand devalued the baht and re-pegged it to a currency basket, ending its fixed dollar peg. This framework held for over a decade until speculative pressure forced a float on 2 July 1997, triggering the Asian Financial Crisis.

tr-1990.blurb: Turkey sided with the US-led coalition against Iraq, closing the Kirkuk-Yumurtalik pipeline and authorising foreign troop deployments — marking a decisive break from its post-WWII non-involvement posture, though the alignment came at heavy economic cost and failed to accelerate EU accession.

tr-2013.blurb: The Gezi Park protests were suppressed by mid-June 2013, with Erdogan branding demonstrators as terrorists; a major corruption scandal followed in December, forcing ministerial resignations, though prosecutions were ultimately blocked and no ministers were tried.

tm-2003.blurb: In August 2003, Turkmenistan's People's Council adopted constitutional amendments making itself the supreme legislative organ above the parliament, stripping the Mejlis of key powers and cementing President Niyazov's grip on power through institutional control rather than a formal "president for life" title.

tm-2015.blurb: Turkmenistan completed its domestic section by around 2018-2019, but the Afghan segment faced deep delays — security instability, financing shortfalls, and absent firm off-take commitments from India and Pakistan left the broader pipeline non-operational for years after the 2015 groundbreaking.

ug-1976.blurb: Following the humiliating Israeli raid on Entebbe, Idi Amin ordered retaliatory killings of Kenyans in Uganda, destroying his regime's international standing and accelerating the regional isolation that culminated in Uganda's defeat in the Uganda–Tanzania War and Amin's overthrow in 1979.

ug-1979.blurb: Tanzania counter-invaded Uganda following Amin's 1978 incursion into the Kagera region; by April 1979, Tanzanian and Ugandan exile forces had taken Kampala, collapsing Idi Amin's eight-year dictatorship and installing a UNLF coalition government under Yusufu Lule.

ug-2006.blurb: In July 2006, Uganda and the LRA opened the Juba Peace Talks under South Sudanese mediation — the most structured negotiations in the conflict's history — but LRA leader Joseph Kony refused to sign the final agreement in April 2008, collapsing the process and triggering a multinational military offensive that December.

gb-1984.blurb: The strike collapsed in March 1985 with miners returning to work without an agreement, and the full pit closure programme proceeded — by 1994 only 15 of the original 174 pits remained open, marking a decisive shift in the balance of power between the Thatcher government and organised labour.

us-1971.blurb: The Bretton Woods fixed-exchange-rate system collapsed in the aftermath, and by 1973 major currencies shifted to a floating exchange rate regime, with the dollar becoming a fully fiat currency and the global monetary order fundamentally reshaped.

us-2011.blurb: The Budget Control Act, signed by President Obama in August 2011 in response to the debt-ceiling crisis, set caps on discretionary spending and created an automatic sequestration mechanism; when a bipartisan "super-committee" failed to reach agreement, mandatory defense cuts took effect in March 2013, fundamentally restructuring US military spending for a decade.

us-2017.blurb: President Trump signed the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act on December 22, 2017 — the largest U.S. tax overhaul since 1986 — permanently cutting the corporate rate from 35% to 21% and projecting roughly $1.5 trillion added to the federal deficit over a decade, while individual tax cuts were set to expire after 2025.

uz-2000.blurb: The Islamic Movement of Uzbekistan's 2000 armed incursion into Kyrgyzstan and southern Uzbekistan was repelled by autumn, with IMU fighters retreating to Taliban-controlled Afghanistan, where most were destroyed in the 2001 US-led campaign; the episode drew Uzbekistan into close US counter-terrorism partnership while Karimov used it to intensify domestic repression.

uz-2014.blurb: In February 2014, Gulnara Karimova — daughter of President Islam Karimov and once his likely successor — was placed under house arrest and investigated for accepting over $1 billion in bribes from foreign telecom companies seeking Uzbekistan market access, effectively ending her political career and triggering asset seizures and criminal proceedings across multiple countries.

ve-1998.blurb: Hugo Chávez won Venezuela's December 1998 presidential election on an anti-corruption, pro-poor platform, took office in February 1999, and swiftly convened a Constituent Assembly that produced a new constitution, redirecting oil revenues to social programs and setting Venezuela on a socialist trajectory that reshaped the country for decades.

ve-2019.blurb: Despite recognition by roughly 60 countries, Guaidó's parallel government never dislodged Maduro, whose control held through sustained military loyalty; the opposition coalition dissolved the interim government in January 2023.

ye-2002.blurb: In November 2002, a CIA Predator drone strike in Marib Governorate killed al-Qaeda's senior Yemen leader al-Harithi — the first US targeted drone strike outside a conventional battlefield — inaugurating a sustained covert-warfare presence in Yemen that expanded significantly after 2009.

ye-2011.blurb: Mass protests in 2011 forced President Ali Abdullah Saleh — in power for over 30 years — to sign a GCC-brokered transfer of power; his vice president Hadi was elected president in February 2012, though the transition ultimately collapsed as the Houthi movement seized Sanaa by late 2014 and civil war followed.

ye-2017.blurb: Following a Houthi ballistic missile strike on Riyadh in November 2017, the Saudi-led coalition imposed a total blockade of Yemen, triggering a catastrophic humanitarian crisis; weeks later, former President Saleh broke with the Houthis, and Houthi fighters killed him as he fled Sanaa in December 2017, shattering their alliance and deepening the conflict's fragmentation.

zm-2005.blurb: In April 2005, Zambia reached the HIPC Completion Point, triggering cancellation of roughly $3.9 billion in nominal debt from the IMF, World Bank, and African Development Bank. The government used the freed fiscal space to eliminate school and healthcare user fees and began providing free antiretroviral drugs to 100,000 Zambians.

zw-2008.blurb: Following a disputed March 2008 election, state-sponsored violence against the MDC opposition forced Tsvangirai to withdraw from the presidential run-off; a SADC-brokered Global Political Agreement was signed in September 2008, leading to a Government of National Unity in February 2009 with Mugabe as President and Tsvangirai as Prime Minister.

af-1982.blurb: In June 1982, the UN launched Geneva proximity talks on Afghanistan, with envoy Diego Cordovez shuttling between the Kabul regime and Pakistan; the six-year process culminated in the April 1988 Geneva Accords, under which the Soviet Union committed to a full troop withdrawal completed by February 1989.

af-1996.blurb: The Taliban seized Kabul in September 1996, overthrowing the Rabbani government and declaring the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan; they publicly executed former president Najibullah and imposed strict sharia, while sheltering al-Qaeda — a harboring relationship that ultimately triggered the US-led invasion in October 2001.

af-2009.blurb: The fraud-marred August 2009 presidential election returned Hamid Karzai to power for a second term, severely damaging the Afghan government's legitimacy; in December 2009, President Obama responded to the deteriorating situation by ordering a surge of 30,000 additional US troops into Afghanistan.

dz-1992.blurb: The military coup ignited the Algerian Civil War (1992–2002), as banned Islamist armed groups launched an insurgency against the state that killed an estimated 150,000–200,000 people over a decade commonly called "the Black Decade."

ao-1990.blurb: In December 1990, the ruling MPLA formally abandoned Marxism-Leninism and accepted multiparty democracy, leading to the 1991 Bicesse Accords peace deal with UNITA and Angola's first multiparty elections in September 1992 — but UNITA's Jonas Savimbi rejected the results and the civil war resumed.

ar-1970.blurb: Levingston's tenure lasted less than a year: worsening inflation, escalating guerrilla violence, and a second Córdoba uprising (the Viborazo) led the junta to depose him in March 1971, eventually paving the way for the 1973 elections that returned Juan Perón to power.

at-2018.blurb: Austria held the EU Council Presidency in the second half of 2018, using it to advance Western Balkans accession and secure dozens of legislative agreements; the European Parliament later assessed it as one of the most successful presidencies in recent EU history.

az-1997.blurb: The OSCE Minsk Group's 1997 peace framework for Nagorno-Karabakh was rejected, and no political resolution followed; the hundreds of thousands of Azerbaijani displaced persons remained in protracted displacement for nearly three decades, until the 2020 Second Nagorno-Karabakh War.

az-2011.blurb: In December 2011, Azerbaijan enacted a landmark overhaul of its Soviet-era conscription system, and by February 2012 a presidential decree replaced the old military commissariats with a new civilian State Service for Mobilization and Conscription, marking the country's most significant military-institutional reform of the post-Soviet era.

bd-2013.blurb: The April 2013 Rana Plaza collapse — killing 1,134 garment workers — prompted murder charges against the building owner, new factory inspection laws, and the landmark Accord on Fire and Building Safety in Bangladesh signed by over 200 global brands.

by-2011.blurb: Following Belarus's disputed December 2010 election, the Lukashenko government arrested hundreds of protesters and cracked down on opposition through 2011; the EU responded with travel bans, asset freezes, and an arms embargo. Most individual sanctions were lifted in February 2016, though the arms embargo continued beyond that date.

by-2017.blurb: Zapad-2017, held September 14–20 on Belarusian territory, revealed deep Russia-Belarus military integration and triggered significant NATO alarm — particularly among Baltic states and Poland — reinforcing the rationale for the alliance's already-established eastern posture.

be-1992.blurb: Belgium signed the Maastricht Treaty on February 7, 1992, becoming a founding member of the European Union when the treaty entered into force in November 1993, with Brussels — already home to key EU institutions — cementing its central role in the new supranational order.

be-2014.blurb: Following the May 2014 federal elections, Belgium's four-party Michel I Government was sworn in on 11 October 2014 — the first coalition since 1988 to include Flemish nationalists — and promptly pursued an austerity programme that triggered one of the country's largest general strikes in decades.

bo-1971.blurb: In August 1971, Colonel Hugo Banzer Suárez seized power in Bolivia through a military coup, ousting President Juan José Torres after three days of fighting. Banzer's takeover inaugurated a seven-year right-wing military dictatorship marked by the suppression of political parties, unions, and universities.

bo-1995.blurb: President Sánchez de Lozada's 90-day state of siege suppressed the general strike, and the capitalization program proceeded — with ENFE and five other state companies transferred to private investors. The repression fueled lasting resentment that fed the 2000 Cochabamba Water War and 2003 Gas War, eventually propelling Evo Morales to the presidency in 2005.

bw-1971.blurb: The Orapa diamond mine began commercial production in July 1971, the final year of direct British financial support, launching Botswana on a trajectory from one of Africa's poorest nations to a middle-income country over the following decades.

bw-1975.blurb: Botswana passed the Bank of Botswana Act in 1975, establishing an independent central bank after withdrawing from the Rand Monetary Area, and on 23 August 1976 introduced its own national currency, the pula, replacing the South African rand.

bw-1993.blurb: In November 1993, Botswana established the Pula Fund — a sovereign wealth fund managed by the Bank of Botswana to invest surplus revenues from diamond royalties, institutionalising the ring-fencing of non-renewable resource proceeds into a long-term savings vehicle rather than current consumption.

bw-1996.blurb: Botswana's HIV/AIDS epidemic, already generalized by 1996, surged toward a peak of nearly 40% prevalence around 2003, collapsing adult life expectancy to under 40 years — prompting one of Africa's first national antiretroviral treatment programs by 2002.

bw-2018.blurb: On 1 April 2018, Mokgweetsi Masisi was sworn in as Botswana's president, succeeding Ian Khama via a constitutional BDP handover. The two men fell out — Khama quit the BDP and endorsed the opposition — but Masisi led the BDP to victory in the October 2019 elections.

br-1995.blurb: In December 1995, President Fernando Henrique Cardoso signed Law No. 9,140, the first law formally acknowledging state responsibility for political killings and disappearances under Brazil's military dictatorship (1964–1985), establishing a reparations commission and opening the country's transitional justice process.

br-2020.blurb: Brazil's economy contracted 3.3% in 2020 as COVID-19 struck, with H1 recording a 7% contraction — the largest in 30 years — and nearly 12 million jobs lost by July. The government's Emergency Aid briefly lifted ~23 million above extreme poverty, but pushed public debt to ~100% of GDP and set up a prolonged fiscal consolidation challenge.

ca-1963.blurb: Lester Pearson's Liberals took power in April 1963, ending six years of Diefenbaker rule, and governed as a minority to deliver Medicare, the Canada Pension Plan, and a new national flag — while the FLQ, founded that same year, escalated its bombing campaign toward the 1970 October Crisis.

ca-1967.blurb: In August 1967, Canada enacted the world's first universal points-based immigration system, replacing race- and national-origin criteria with a merit score across nine categories. The shift fundamentally reoriented the source regions of Canadian immigration and became the global template for skills-based admissions.

ca-1970.blurb: Prime Minister Trudeau invoked the War Measures Act — the only peacetime invocation in Canadian history — deploying the military across Quebec and suspending habeas corpus; Pierre Laporte was murdered by his captors, while James Cross was eventually released. The crisis discredited violent separatism, and democratic nationalism through the Parti Québécois supplanted the FLQ, culminating in the PQ's 1976 Quebec election victory.

ca-1998.blurb: The storm triggered Canada's largest-ever peacetime military deployment — over 15,000 troops under Operation Recuperation — exposed critical gaps in emergency infrastructure, and prompted redesigned transmission towers and centralized grid management, reshaping Canadian emergency management doctrine for decades.

ca-2001.blurb: Canada responded with sweeping anti-terrorism legislation (the Anti-Terrorism Act, royal assent December 2001) and the Smart Border Declaration with the US, a 30-point plan restructuring bilateral border management for two decades through trusted-traveller and pre-clearance programs.

ca-2021.blurb: Canada established September 30 as a federal statutory National Day for Truth and Reconciliation and pledged funding for grave identification. In July 2022, Pope Francis traveled to Canada and issued a formal apology for the Catholic Church's role in the residential school system.

cn-1983.blurb: By the end of 1983, China's Household Responsibility System had reached near-universal adoption across rural households, completing the decollectivization of agriculture and generating sufficient political and economic confidence to extend market-oriented reforms to urban industry and Special Economic Zones from 1984 onward.

cn-1989.blurb: The crackdown triggered international sanctions and an EU arms embargo that remains in place; domestically, the Communist Party purged reformist leaders, imprisoned thousands of dissidents, and consolidated authoritarian rule under Jiang Zemin, cementing a reform-without-democratization trajectory.

cn-2012.blurb: At the 18th National Congress in November 2012, Xi Jinping succeeded Hu Jintao as General Secretary of the CCP and Chairman of the Central Military Commission, launching a sweeping anti-corruption campaign and an assertive foreign policy posture that defined the subsequent decade of Chinese governance.

cn-2017.blurb: Beginning in 2017, China launched a mass detention campaign targeting Uyghurs and other Turkic Muslims in Xinjiang, incarcerating an estimated one million people without trial; the system expanded through 2018–2019, drawing international condemnation and ultimately a U.S. genocide designation in 2021.

co-1972.blurb: The Chicoral Pact formally reversed Colombia's redistributive land reform agenda, producing laws in 1973 that shielded large landholdings from expropriation and directed state credit toward large landowners — entrenching land concentration and deepening rural grievances that sustained insurgencies for decades.

co-1984.blurb: The assassination shocked President Betancur into reversing his opposition to extradition; by November 1984, Colombia formally activated the 1979 bilateral extradition treaty with the United States, triggering a decade-long violent conflict between the state and the Medellín Cartel.

co-2003.blurb: The February 2003 El Nogal Club bombing — attributed to FARC — killed 36 people and galvanised public support behind President Uribe's Democratic Security policy, accelerating a counterinsurgency campaign that forced FARC into retreat and reduced violence across Colombia through the mid-2000s.

cr-2011.blurb: The Costa Rica–China Free Trade Agreement entered into force on August 1, 2011 — the first such pact China signed with any Central American country — making China Costa Rica's second-largest trade partner, though a persistent structural trade deficit soon followed.

cu-1980.blurb: Between April and October 1980, roughly 125,000 Cubans reached Florida in the Mariel Boatlift after Castro opened the port of Mariel, prompting the Carter administration to declare a state of emergency and triggering a sharp backlash that hardened US public opinion on immigration from Cuba and Latin America.

cy-1990.blurb: In July 1990, Cyprus formally applied for membership in the European Economic Community, launching a path toward EU accession that culminated in Cyprus joining as a full member state on 1 May 2004, though the island remained divided at entry.

dk-2021.blurb: In 2021, Denmark implemented the Arctic Capability Package and built cross-party consensus around ending its EU defence opt-out; this culminated in a June 2022 referendum in which ~67% of Danes voted to scrap the 30-year exemption, and Denmark joined EU defence cooperation on 1 July 2022.

ec-2021.blurb: Guillermo Lasso won Ecuador's April 2021 presidential runoff with 52% of the vote but led a minority government facing chronic legislative deadlock. In May 2023 he invoked the "muerte cruzada" mechanism, dissolving the National Assembly and triggering snap elections that brought a new president to power.

eg-1961.blurb: Nasser's July 1961 socialist decrees, nationalizing banks and industry across the United Arab Republic, alienated Syria's propertied classes; eight weeks later Syrian army units staged a coup and seceded, dissolving the UAR and dealing a severe blow to pan-Arab unification.

sv-2009.blurb: Mauricio Funes of the former guerrilla movement FMLN took office on June 1, 2009, ending 20 consecutive years of ARENA rule — the first peaceful transfer of power from right to left in El Salvador's modern history and a widely recognised milestone in the country's post-civil-war democratic consolidation.

sv-2020.blurb: Bukele's pandemic-era defiance of court rulings and suspension of constitutional rights accelerated his authoritarian consolidation; in May 2021, his party won a legislative supermajority and immediately replaced the Supreme Court justices and Attorney General, marking a widely condemned democratic backsliding milestone.

sv-2021.blurb: After Bukele's party swept the 2021 elections, the new assembly dismissed the Supreme Court's constitutional magistrates and the attorney general, consolidating executive control. It then swiftly passed a Bitcoin legal tender law, making El Salvador the first country to adopt cryptocurrency as legal tender — a move the IMF opposed and that was reversed in 2025.

er-1979.blurb: Ethiopia launched its 4th and 5th offensives against Eritrean independence forces in 1979, combining scorched-earth tactics with aerial bombardment that drove a mass refugee exodus into eastern Sudan — swelling the displaced population to roughly 390,000 by late 1979.

er-1985.blurb: By 1985, the intersection of severe drought and Ethiopian scorched-earth warfare had driven approximately 250,000 Eritreans into Sudan as refugees, straining regional humanitarian systems and drawing international attention through the Band Aid/Live Aid response.

er-1998.blurb: Eritrea's seizure of the disputed border town of Badme in May 1998 triggered a full-scale war with Ethiopia that lasted until June 2000, killing tens of thousands and displacing hundreds of thousands, while entrenching President Isaias Afwerki's authoritarian rule and imposing indefinite national military conscription.

er-1999.blurb: Ethiopia's Operation Sunset in February 1999 decisively broke Eritrean lines at Badme, forcing a retreat and Eritrea's acceptance of an OAU peace plan; by mid-2000, over one million people had been displaced and an estimated 100,000 soldiers killed across the two-year war.

er-2001.blurb: The crackdown permanently ended all independent media in Eritrea, cancelled scheduled elections indefinitely, and left the arrested G-15 officials and journalists held incommunicado without charge for decades, consolidating the country into one of the world's most repressive single-party states.

er-2014.blurb: In June 2014, the UN Human Rights Council established a Commission of Inquiry on Human Rights in Eritrea to investigate systematic abuses including forced conscription, torture, and enforced disappearances; by 2016 the Commission concluded that crimes against humanity had been committed across the country since 1991, deepening Eritrea's international isolation.

er-2017.blurb: When Qatar withdrew its peacekeeping contingent from the Eritrea–Djibouti border in June 2017 — a fallout from the Gulf diplomatic crisis — the 2010 Doha Agreement mediation framework collapsed, Eritrean forces moved into the disputed Ras Doumeira terrain, and the two countries were left in a direct, unmediated military standoff with no replacement mediator emerging through year's end.

et-1973.blurb: The famine's exposure fatally undermined Haile Selassie's government; in September 1974, a Marxist military junta known as the Derg overthrew him, ending 44 years of imperial rule and triggering prolonged civil war and insurgency that dominated Ethiopian politics for two decades.

et-2003.blurb: Following the December 2003 Gambella massacre, military attacks on Anuak villages continued into 2004–2005; no senior officials were held accountable, and a government inquiry absolved the military, drawing sustained international condemnation from Human Rights Watch and Genocide Watch.

et-2004.blurb: Eritrea rejected Ethiopia's November 2004 Five-Point Peace Plan outright, and the border demarcation remained frozen as the two countries endured a "no war, no peace" standoff for another fourteen years, until the 2018 peace agreement under Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed.

fr-1980.blurb: The bombing sparked mass anti-racist demonstrations across France and marked a turning point in the country's awareness of antisemitic terrorism, while judicial proceedings stretched across decades — culminating in a controversial 2023 conviction in absentia of a Lebanese-Canadian suspect.

fr-1986.blurb: Following the March 1986 legislative elections, President François Mitterrand was compelled to appoint RPR leader Jacques Chirac as Prime Minister — the Fifth Republic's first cohabitation — establishing a precedent for divided executive power that endured until Mitterrand's re-election in May 1988.

fr-2018.blurb: Facing mass weekly protests from the leaderless Gilets Jaunes movement, President Macron cancelled the fuel tax hike and announced a minimum wage increase in December 2018, though demonstrations continued into 2020 as protesters argued the underlying inequalities remained unaddressed.

gh-1994.blurb: The Rawlings government declared a state of emergency and deployed military forces; a ceasefire was signed in June 1994, though fighting resumed in 1995. The conflict formally ended with the Kumasi Accord for Peace and Reconciliation, signed on 30 March 1996.

gr-2010.blurb: In May 2010, the EU, ECB, and IMF agreed to a €110 billion bailout for Greece conditioned on sweeping austerity measures; the resulting recession lasted until 2017, with two further bailout programs following in 2012 and 2015.

ht-1985.blurb: The killings sparked a nationwide uprising known as the Dechoukaj, and on February 7, 1986, Jean-Claude "Baby Doc" Duvalier fled to France, ending nearly 30 years of dynastic Duvalier rule and handing power to a military junta.

ht-1988.blurb: The St. Jean Bosco church massacre triggered the September 18, 1988 coup that ousted General Namphy and brought General Avril to power, while elevating Father Aristide's profile — setting the stage for his landslide presidential election victory in December 1990.

hn-1974.blurb: The scandal broke in early 1975 when United Brands CEO Eli Black died by suicide, prompting an SEC investigation that uncovered the bribe, leading to López Arellano's removal and contributing directly to the U.S. Foreign Corrupt Practices Act of 1977.

is-1990.blurb: In February 1990, Iceland's government and labour partners struck a landmark wage stabilization pact — unions accepted lower nominal increases while the government committed to curbing inflation — breaking decisively from the high-inflation era and launching a decade of liberalization and strong growth.

in-1974.blurb: The government's crushing of the strike — through mass detentions and dismissals — became one of the precipitating events leading Indira Gandhi to declare the Emergency in June 1975; in the subsequent 1977 elections, Gandhi lost her seat while strike leader George Fernandes won from prison.

in-1984.blurb: Following Operation Blue Star, Prime Minister Indira Gandhi was assassinated by her Sikh bodyguards on 31 October 1984; the killing triggered anti-Sikh pogroms across India and a sympathy wave that carried her son Rajiv Gandhi and Congress (I) to a historic landslide in the December 1984 general election.

in-2004.blurb: The BJP-led NDA's "India Shining" campaign suffered a major upset defeat in the April–May 2004 general election, with the Congress-led United Progressive Alliance forming government and Manmohan Singh becoming Prime Minister — marking Congress's return to power after six years in opposition.

in-2008.blurb: India suspended composite dialogue with Pakistan, demanded dismantling of Lashkar-e-Taiba infrastructure, and overhauled domestic security institutions — establishing the National Investigation Agency and amending anti-terror legislation — in the months following the November 2008 Mumbai attacks.

in-2012.blurb: In September 2014, India's Supreme Court declared the entire coal block allocation process since 1993 illegal and cancelled 214 of 218 allocations; the government replaced discretionary allocation with competitive auctions, and the scandal is widely credited with contributing to the UPA's defeat in the 2014 general election.

id-2002.blurb: Following the October 2002 Bali bombings, Indonesia enacted counterterrorism legislation, established Densus 88 with Western support, and expanded intelligence-sharing. Subsequent arrests decimated Jemaah Islamiyah and fractured it between pro- and anti-bombing factions, severely weakening its operational capacity.

id-2014.blurb: Joko Widodo's victory in the July 2014 presidential election — Indonesia's first won by someone outside the military or political elite — triggered a landmark fiscal reform: within two months of taking office, Jokowi cut fuel subsidies and effectively removed the gasoline subsidy, redirecting the freed budget space toward infrastructure investment.

ir-1962.blurb: The land redistribution provoked fierce clerical opposition: Khomeini denounced the reforms, was arrested in June 1963 after his Ashura speech triggered the 15 Khordad uprising, and was exiled in 1964 — a trajectory that led directly to the 1979 Islamic Revolution.

ir-1965.blurb: The Shah swiftly appointed Finance Minister Amir-Abbas Hoveyda as Prime Minister — a tenure spanning over twelve years — while Bokharaei and three co-conspirators were arrested and executed, and the regime intensified SAVAK crackdowns on Islamist opposition networks.

iq-1958.blurb: In July 1958, General Abd al-Karim Qasim and the Free Officers overthrew Iraq's Hashemite monarchy, killing King Faisal II and establishing the Iraqi Republic; Qasim swiftly enacted agrarian reform breaking up feudal landholdings and redistributed land to peasant families.

iq-1975.blurb: Iran's withdrawal of support immediately collapsed the Kurdish rebellion; Iraq then launched a military campaign against the Kurds and extended state control over Iraqi Kurdistan. Saddam Hussein abrogated the accord in September 1980 and invaded Iran, triggering the Iran-Iraq War.

iq-1991.blurb: Following Iraq's defeat in the Gulf War, a simultaneous Kurdish and Shia uprising in March 1991 was crushed by Saddam Hussein's Republican Guard, triggering a refugee crisis that displaced roughly two million Kurds; international intervention established a northern no-fly zone, leading to de facto Kurdish autonomy and the Kurdistan Regional Government's first elections in 1992.

iq-2018.blurb: Mass protests over contaminated water, power outages, and unemployment swept Basra from July–September 2018. The political deadlock ended when independent Shia politician Adel Abdul-Mahdi was nominated Prime Minister on 2 October 2018. Basra's grievances went unresolved, seeding the nationwide Tishreen uprising of 2019.

il-2010.blurb: The raid sparked an immediate diplomatic rupture: Turkey expelled Israel's ambassador and demanded an apology, compensation, and an end to the Gaza blockade — a standoff that lasted until Netanyahu's formal apology in March 2013 and a compensation agreement in 2016, permanently damaging one of the region's most significant Muslim-majority–Israeli alliances.

it-1991.blurb: Italy forcibly detained and deported most of the Vlora's passengers within days, establishing a strict non-admission and rapid-deportation doctrine that became a founding precedent for European debates on mass irregular migration and forced repatriation.

jm-2002.blurb: In the October 2002 general election, Prime Minister P.J. Patterson and the People's National Party won 34 of 60 parliamentary seats, making Patterson the first Jamaican leader to win three successive general elections and securing his fourth consecutive term as Prime Minister.

jp-1980.blurb: Japan's economy crossed $1 trillion in nominal GDP in 1980, cementing its standing as the world's second-largest economy — a high-water mark that preceded the late-1980s asset bubble, whose collapse ushered in the "Lost Decades" of stagnation through the 1990s and 2000s.

jp-1999.blurb: The BOJ lifted its zero interest rate policy in August 2000, but the recovery proved short-lived; deflationary pressures returned, and by March 2001 Japan had adopted full quantitative easing — the first QE programme by any central bank in modern history.

jp-2019.blurb: Emperor Akihito abdicated on 30 April 2019 — the first Japanese imperial abdication in roughly 200 years — and Crown Prince Naruhito ascended the Chrysanthemum Throne on 1 May 2019, inaugurating the Reiwa era in a peaceful, constitutionally managed transition.

jo-1997.blurb: In Jordan's November 1997 parliamentary elections, the Islamic Action Front led an 11-party opposition boycott over the one-person, one-vote electoral law and press restrictions; independents swept 75 of 80 seats on 45% turnout, leaving the IAF isolated from formal politics until 2003.

jo-2000.blurb: In October 2000, Jordan and the United States signed the first free trade agreement between the US and any Arab country; it entered into force in December 2001, spurring a sharp rise in Jordanian exports to the US and the creation of roughly 30,000 jobs in export manufacturing.

jo-2019.blurb: On November 10, 2019, Jordan reclaimed full sovereignty over the Baqoura and Al-Ghamr enclaves as Annex I of the 1994 Wadi Araba peace treaty expired, ending Israeli agricultural access after 25 years and marking Jordan's first tangible territorial reassertion under the treaty framework.

kz-2000.blurb: In August 2000, President Nazarbayev established the National Fund of Kazakhstan by decree to save oil export revenues and buffer the budget from commodity volatility, receiving its first deposit of $660 million in January 2001 and growing into the central instrument of Kazakhstan's sovereign wealth management.

ke-1980.blurb: In April 1980, Kenya signed one of the World Bank's first-ever structural adjustment loans — a $55 million IDA credit conditioned on currency devaluation, tariff reduction, and austerity measures — initiating a decades-long cycle of SAP-conditioned borrowing that curtailed social spending and reoriented the economy toward export extraction.

ke-2014.blurb: On 5 December 2014, ICC Prosecutor Fatou Bensouda withdrew all charges against President Uhuru Kenyatta — citing Kenya's deliberate non-cooperation and witness disappearances — closing the case without acquittal or conviction and leaving perpetrators of the 2007–08 post-election violence effectively unpunished.

kw-2011.blurb: After protesters stormed the National Assembly in November 2011 over corruption allegations, Prime Minister Sheikh Nasser Al-Mohammad resigned within days; snap elections followed but the results were annulled by the Constitutional Court, inaugurating a prolonged cycle of parliamentary dissolutions and political gridlock.

kw-2020.blurb: Emir Sheikh Sabah al-Ahmad al-Sabah died on 29 September 2020, and Sheikh Nawaf al-Ahmad al-Sabah was sworn in the following day, inheriting a country in fiscal stress and legislative gridlock that would produce three parliamentary elections in as many years — a governance crisis that persisted until his own death in December 2023.

la-1992.blurb: Following the death of founding president Kaysone Phomvihane in November 1992 and Laos's first parliamentary election under its new constitution that December, Khamtai Siphandon consolidated power as LPRP chairman while Nouhak Phoumsavan became state president, cementing single-party rule into the following decade.

lv-2017.blurb: In June 2017, NATO stood up a Canadian-led Enhanced Forward Presence battlegroup in Latvia at Camp Ādaži — over 1,000 troops from six allied nations — marking NATO's largest reinforcement of its eastern flank since the Cold War and locking Latvia into a sustained upward military spending trajectory.

lv-2018.blurb: In February 2018, Latvia's ABLV Bank collapsed after the U.S. Treasury designated it a primary money laundering concern, triggering a bank run and ECB moratorium; ABLV's board voted for voluntary liquidation, and the episode became a landmark case in the EU debate over centralising anti-money-laundering supervision.

ly-1999.blurb: In April 1999, Libya handed over the two Lockerbie bombing suspects to Scottish authorities for trial in the Netherlands, prompting the UN Security Council to immediately suspend the multilateral sanctions it had imposed on Libya since 1992.

mg-1991.blurb: Presidential guards opened fire on a mass protest march in August 1991, killing dozens and fatally undermining Ratsiraka's authority; a transitional agreement stripped him of power that October, and Albert Zafy won the presidency in 1993, ending 17 years of single-party rule.

at-2010.blurb: Austria's Federal Budget Reform Stage 1, in force from 2009, introduced binding four-year expenditure ceilings and carryover rights for unspent funds; Stage 2 added performance and accrual budgeting in 2013, earning Austria IMF recognition as a comprehensive public financial management reformer.

my-2007.blurb: The 2007 Bersih and HINDRAF rallies catalysed a political earthquake in Malaysia's March 2008 general election, in which the ruling Barisan Nasional coalition lost its parliamentary two-thirds supermajority — held continuously since 1969 — for the first time in nearly 40 years.

ml-1991.blurb: Following the March Revolution, Lieutenant Colonel Amadou Toumani Touré oversaw a democratic transition that legalized opposition parties and produced Mali's first multiparty elections in 1992, in which Alpha Oumar Konaré was elected president and Touré peacefully transferred power.

ml-2007.blurb: In January 2007, the GSPC formally rebranded as Al-Qaeda in the Islamic Maghreb (AQIM) and immediately expanded operations southward into the Sahel, using northern Mali as a base — a transformation that, compounded by a concurrent Tuareg rebellion, laid the groundwork for Mali's 2012 territorial crisis and the French military intervention.

mu-2011.blurb: The MedPoint hospital corruption scandal led to the arrest of Health Minister Maya Hanoomanjee in July 2011 and the resignation of all six MSM cabinet ministers, collapsing the Labour–MSM coalition and weakening PM Ramgoolam's government through the 2014 election cycle.

mu-2021.blurb: Facing a coalition of over 50 civil society organizations, the Mauritian government did not advance the proposed ICT Act amendments to legislation in 2021. The consultation paper was removed from the ICTA website, effectively shelving the proposal under sustained domestic and international pressure.

mx-1959.blurb: President López Mateos crushed the railroad workers' strike in March 1959, deploying the military to seize rail stations and imprisoning leader Demetrio Vallejo for over eleven years — establishing a lasting precedent for state repression of independent unionism in Mexico.

mx-1972.blurb: The counter-insurgency campaign drove hundreds of disappearances and killings, pushing surviving guerrilla factions to merge into the Liga Comunista 23 de Septiembre in 1973; armed struggle continued until a 1978 amnesty ended most militant activity.

mx-1990.blurb: In 1990, President Carlos Salinas de Gortari privatized Telmex, selling the state telephone monopoly to a group led by Carlos Slim — the largest privatization in Mexican history — transferring a public monopoly into private hands and launching one of the world's great fortunes.

mx-2016.blurb: Mexico signed the Trans-Pacific Partnership in February 2016, but when the US withdrew in January 2017, the deal collapsed; Mexico pivoted to join the surviving nations in the CPTPP, which entered into force for Mexico in December 2018, while simultaneously navigating the NAFTA renegotiation that ultimately produced USMCA in 2020.

mn-2011.blurb: Mongolia became the world's fastest-growing economy in 2011, powered by a mining boom anchored by the Oyu Tolgoi copper-gold mega-project and surging coal exports — but the wealth influx triggered a political backlash, and by 2012 the government was suspending mining licenses and seeking to renegotiate terms with foreign investors.

mn-2019.blurb: In November 2019, Mongolia enacted its most significant constitutional amendments since 1992, reducing the presidential term to a single non-renewable six-year term and granting the prime minister autonomous cabinet appointment powers, rebalancing a tripartite power structure that had generated chronic instability for over two decades.

ma-1956.blurb: Within months of France ending its protectorate in March 1956, King Mohammed V issued a royal decree establishing the Royal Armed Forces, integrating repatriated Moroccan soldiers from French and Spanish forces alongside liberation army guerrillas and centralising military command under the crown.

ma-1975.blurb: Within weeks of the Green March, Spain, Morocco, and Mauritania signed the Madrid Accords (November 14, 1975), transferring Western Sahara to joint Moroccan-Mauritanian administration — triggering a guerrilla war by the Polisario Front that left the territory's sovereignty unresolved for decades.

ma-1976.blurb: Following Spain's withdrawal and the Polisario Front's proclamation of the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic in February 1976, Morocco entered a sustained guerrilla war over Western Sahara; Mauritania eventually renounced its share of the territory in 1979, and a UN ceasefire in 1991 left the conflict formally unresolved.

ma-2021.blurb: In August 2021, Algeria severed diplomatic relations with Morocco over a series of alleged hostile actions, and subsequently closed the Maghreb-Europe Gas Pipeline transiting Morocco in November 2021, cutting off Morocco's transit revenues and disrupting gas supplies to Spain.

mz-1987.blurb: In January 1987, Mozambique launched the IMF/World Bank-backed Programa de Reabilitação Económica, formally abandoning its Marxist-Leninist planned economy for a market system through price liberalization, currency devaluation, and privatization — setting the country on a sustained growth trajectory through the mid-1990s.

mz-2015.blurb: When the hidden debts were revealed in 2016, the IMF suspended its loan program and Western donors followed, triggering a sovereign default and prolonged economic crisis that defined Mozambique's financial trajectory for years.

mm-1983.blurb: Burma severed diplomatic relations with North Korea and expelled its diplomats following the October 1983 Rangoon bombing, a rupture that lasted until 2007.

mm-2005.blurb: In November 2005, Myanmar's military junta abruptly relocated the national capital from Yangon to the newly built, heavily fortified city of Naypyidaw, physically isolating the government from the civilian population and entrenching military rule through subsequent transitions and the 2021 coup.

np-1989.blurb: India's 1989 trade and transit blockade inflicted severe economic hardship on Nepal, fueling domestic unrest that erupted in the Jana Andolan — a 50-day mass uprising in early 1990 that forced King Birendra to dismantle the Panchayat system and transition Nepal to a multi-party constitutional democracy.

np-2006.blurb: The 19-day Jana Andolan II uprising forced King Gyanendra to reinstate parliament in April 2006 and surrender near-all royal powers; a Comprehensive Peace Accord signed in November ended a decade-long civil war, and the monarchy was formally abolished in 2008.

nz-1999.blurb: Labour's Helen Clark defeated PM Jenny Shipley in the November 1999 general election, becoming New Zealand's first elected woman Prime Minister and forming a coalition government that ended fifteen years of market-oriented economic reform.

nz-2001.blurb: In 2001, New Zealand established Kiwibank as a state-owned retail bank under New Zealand Post, providing a domestically-owned alternative to the foreign banks that had come to dominate the sector following deregulation and privatisations in the 1980s and 1990s.

ng-1967.blurb: Nigeria's federal government rejected Biafra's declaration of independence and launched a military invasion in July 1967; after three years of war, blockade, and famine that killed over one million people, Biafra surrendered in January 1970 and Nigeria was reunified under federal authority.

kp-1998.blurb: In September 1998, North Korea adopted a revised constitution that abolished the presidency, enshrined Kim Il Sung as "Eternal President," and elevated the National Defence Commission to supreme state power — formally installing Kim Jong-il as de facto leader and codifying military-first governance as the constitutional foundation of the state.

no-2015.blurb: Norway received over 31,000 asylum applications in 2015 — the largest single-year influx in its history — prompting an 18-point cross-party deal that tightened border controls and accelerated returns, after which asylum arrivals fell sharply in early 2016.

pk-1985.blurb: Pakistan held non-party elections in February 1985 under General Zia ul-Haq, with hand-picked Prime Minister Muhammad Khan Junejo taking office; martial law was formally lifted in December 1985, ending eight years of direct military rule, though Zia retained the power to dissolve parliament and the military preserved effective supremacy.

pk-2012.blurb: Malala survived and was evacuated to the UK for treatment; the attack drew worldwide condemnation, prompted Pakistan to pass a compulsory education law, and propelled Malala to become the youngest-ever Nobel Peace Prize laureate in 2014.

ps-2006.blurb: Hamas won a decisive majority in the January 2006 Palestinian legislative elections, ending four decades of Fatah dominance. The US, EU, and Israel immediately imposed sanctions and suspended aid, triggering an economic crisis and escalating internal violence that culminated in Hamas seizing control of Gaza in June 2007.

py-1982.blurb: When the Itaipu dam's construction boom ended in 1982, Paraguay lost its primary growth engine; compounded by collapsing cotton and soybean prices and the Latin American debt crisis, the country entered a prolonged economic slump lasting through 1988, marked by stagnating growth, rising inflation, and deteriorating public finances.

py-2017.blurb: Facing mass protests — including the torching of the Congress building — and domestic and international pressure, President Cartes renounced a second term in April 2017, and the Chamber of Deputies formally rejected the constitutional amendment, leaving Paraguay's re-election ban intact.

pl-2008.blurb: Poland became the only EU member state to avoid recession during the 2008–2009 global financial crisis, sustaining positive GDP growth through a combination of fiscal stimulus, currency depreciation, and accelerated EU structural fund deployment — an outcome widely labelled the "Polish economic miracle."

pl-2021.blurb: Beginning in summer 2021, Belarus deliberately funneled thousands of migrants toward Poland's border in retaliation for EU sanctions, prompting Poland to declare a state of emergency, deploy the military, and erect a permanent border fence, while the EU condemned the action as hybrid warfare and imposed further sanctions on Minsk.

pt-2013.blurb: President Cavaco Silva rejected snap elections and approved a reshuffled coalition, allowing Prime Minister Passos Coelho's government to survive the July 2013 crisis. Portugal completed its EU/IMF bailout programme and exited in May 2014, though the political fallout contributed to the centre-right coalition's defeat in the 2015 elections.

qa-1995.blurb: Crown Prince Hamad bin Khalifa Al Thani deposed his father in a bloodless palace coup on 27 June 1995, proclaiming himself Emir while Khalifa was abroad; a counter-coup attempt in early 1996 failed, and Qatar subsequently pursued an assertive, independent foreign policy that broke from Saudi-led GCC consensus.

ro-2005.blurb: Romania signed the EU Treaty of Accession in April 2005, committing to judicial and anti-corruption reforms under binding pre-accession conditions, and achieved full EU membership on 1 January 2007, accompanied by an ongoing Cooperation and Verification Mechanism to monitor continued compliance.

ru-1953.blurb: Stalin's death in March 1953 triggered a power struggle that ended with the arrest and execution of secret police chief Lavrentiy Beria by December 1953; Nikita Khrushchev ultimately prevailed, subordinating the security apparatus to the party and launching de-Stalinization.

ru-2012.blurb: Putin's return to the presidency triggered the largest post-Soviet protest wave and a systematic crackdown on civil society, including a "foreign agent" law targeting NGOs; the concurrent U.S. Magnitsky Act prompted Russian retaliation and entrenched a sustained authoritarian turn and deterioration of US-Russia relations.

ru-2018.blurb: Putin secured a fourth presidential term in March 2018, extending his rule through 2024, though international monitors condemned the vote as lacking genuine competition; the election laid the groundwork for 2020 constitutional amendments that reset his term limits, enabling him to remain in office potentially until 2036.

rw-2000.blurb: Following President Bizimungu's resignation, Paul Kagame was elected president by parliament in April 2000, consolidating RPF rule and launching Vision 2020 — a long-horizon development framework that drove Rwanda's sustained economic transformation over the following two decades.

rw-2019.blurb: In April 2019, Rwanda marked Kwibuka25 — the 25th anniversary of the genocide against the Tutsi — with President Kagame urging survivors to continue forgiving perpetrators, reinforcing international pressure on countries harboring genocide fugitives and Rwanda's standing as a model of post-atrocity transitional justice.

sa-2003.blurb: The bombings triggered a sweeping Saudi counterterrorism crackdown — over 600 suspects arrested, terrorism financing networks frozen, and intelligence cooperation with the United States intensified — effectively suppressing al-Qaeda within Saudi borders by 2005 and forcing remaining elements to relocate to Yemen.

sa-2005.blurb: Saudi Arabia joined the World Trade Organization on December 11, 2005, becoming its 149th member after more than twelve years of negotiations, triggering sweeping trade liberalization including 42 new laws and expanded foreign investment access.

sa-2010.blurb: Congress cleared the deal with minimal opposition, and over the subsequent decade Saudi Arabia's expanded air and land strike capacity shaped its military posture — most visibly in the 2015 Yemen coalition — reinforcing the US-Saudi bilateral defence architecture.

sa-2016.blurb: In April 2016, Saudi Arabia launched Vision 2030 under Deputy Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, a sweeping reform program to reduce oil dependency through subsidy cuts, economic diversification, and political consolidation — with VAT, partial Aramco privatization, and sector liberalization following in subsequent years.

sn-1983.blurb: Senegal's 1980–1984 structural adjustment program delivered partial fiscal stabilization but failed to restore growth, prompting a deeper second round of reforms — the New Industrial Policy from 1986 — and a decade-long cycle of successive adjustment programs culminating in the CFA franc devaluation of 1994.

sl-2015.blurb: On November 7, 2015, the WHO declared Sierra Leone Ebola-free, ending an outbreak that killed thousands and left the economy in severe recession, with lasting poverty and food insecurity well into 2016.

sg-2001.blurb: Singapore's Internal Security Department detained the 13 arrested JI members without trial under the Internal Security Act, with a second wave of 21 arrests following in August 2002 that authorities assessed had severely crippled the JI network in Singapore and prompted broader regional counterterrorism cooperation.

sk-2015.blurb: Slovakia and Hungary jointly challenged the EU's mandatory refugee relocation scheme at the European Court of Justice, but in September 2017 the ECJ Grand Chamber rejected the case, affirming the quota system's validity and leaving Slovakia legally obligated to accept its assigned asylum seekers.

za-2002.blurb: South Africa enacted the Immigration Act 13 of 2002, replacing the Aliens Control Act and establishing a skills-based migration framework that would anchor the country's immigration policy for years — though its limited provision for unskilled migrants left enforcement gaps as Zimbabwean migration surged.

lk-1962.blurb: Ceylon nationalized its petroleum sector in 1961–1962 under Prime Minister Sirimavo Bandaranaike, expropriating Shell, Esso, and Caltex; the US responded by invoking the Hickenlooper Amendment and suspending foreign aid in 1963, accelerating Ceylon's turn toward non-aligned socialist economic policies.

lk-2009.blurb: Sri Lanka's government declared total military victory over the LTTE on 18–19 May 2009, ending a 26-year civil war, but approximately 300,000 Tamil civilians were interned in military-run displacement camps under heavily criticized conditions, and no credible accountability process for alleged wartime atrocities had been established as of 2024.

sd-2013.blurb: When Sudan's government removed fuel subsidies in September 2013, nationwide protests were met with live fire from security forces, killing at least 185 people. The crackdown suppressed the uprising but entrenched grievances that fueled the 2018–2019 protests that toppled Bashir in April 2019.

sd-2015.blurb: In 2015, President al-Bashir publicly consolidated the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) under Hemedti, and the UAE brokered the paramilitary's first extraterritorial deployment to Yemen — a trajectory that culminated in the RSF's formal legal institutionalization in 2017 and, ultimately, the SAF-RSF civil war of 2023.

ch-1998.blurb: The June 1998 merger of Union Bank of Switzerland and Swiss Bank Corporation created UBS AG, then the world's second-largest bank — but the newly merged institution was immediately struck by massive losses from exposure to the collapse of hedge fund Long-Term Capital Management, forcing the resignation of chairman Mathis Cabiallavetta and three other senior executives.

ch-2017.blurb: In May 2017, Swiss voters approved the Energy Strategy 2050 by a 58% majority, banning new nuclear power plants and committing Switzerland to a long-term transition toward renewables; the Federal Energy Act entered into force on 1 January 2018.

ch-2018.blurb: Swiss voters decisively rejected the SVP's Self-Determination Initiative in November 2018 by 66% to 34%, preserving Switzerland's integration of international law — including the European Convention on Human Rights — with domestic law and delivering a clear defeat for the sovereigntist agenda.

sy-1976.blurb: Syria intervened militarily in Lebanon in mid-1976, deploying tens of thousands of troops to prevent a PLO-leftist victory; legitimized by the Arab League's Arab Deterrent Force in October 1976, Syria's military presence endured for 29 years, establishing it as Lebanon's de facto hegemon until 2005.

sy-2013.blurb: Syrian government forces launched a sarin attack on Ghouta suburbs in August 2013, killing over 1,000 civilians — the deadliest chemical weapons use since 1988. The UN Security Council unanimously passed Resolution 2118 requiring destruction of Syria's chemical arsenal under OPCW supervision, though Syria never fully complied.

tz-2001.blurb: Tanzania's role as host of the Arusha peace process culminated in November 2001 when Burundi inaugurated its transitional government under a Tutsi-Hutu power-sharing arrangement, with South African protection troops deployed to enable the transition — marking the beginning of the end of Burundi's civil war.

th-2015.blurb: Two Uyghur men convicted of the August 2015 Erawan Shrine bombing — which killed 20 people and was Thailand's deadliest in modern history — were sentenced to death by a Bangkok court in June 2026, after one of Thailand's longest-running criminal trials.

tn-2008.blurb: Suppressed by security forces, the 2008 Gafsa uprising nonetheless became Tunisia's most significant protest movement since 1984, and the regional union networks forged during it directly coordinated the 2010–2011 Jasmine Revolution that ousted Ben Ali and ignited the Arab Spring.

tr-2010.blurb: Turkish voters approved 26 constitutional amendments in September 2010, weakening the military's judicial immunity and restructuring the courts — changes that initially accelerated prosecutions of senior officers but ultimately strengthened AKP's grip on the judiciary.

ae-2011.blurb: Five UAE activists arrested in April 2011 for signing a reform petition and criticizing officials online — the "UAE 5" — were sentenced by a security court in November 2011, then quickly pardoned, but the crackdown escalated into mass arrests of 50+ activists by 2012 and a trial of 94 defendants in 2013.

gb-1961.blurb: In August 1961, Prime Minister Harold Macmillan's government formally applied for EEC membership — a sharp break with post-war British policy — but French President Charles de Gaulle vetoed the application in January 1963, and the UK did not join until 1973.

gb-1978.blurb: Ford workers' victory triggered the Winter of Discontent, a wave of strikes that brought down the Callaghan government in a no-confidence vote, leading to Margaret Thatcher's Conservative election win in May 1979.

gb-2003.blurb: No weapons of mass destruction were found after the invasion, and the 2016 Chilcot Inquiry concluded the decision to go to war was not a last resort and was based on overstated intelligence — permanently damaging Tony Blair's political legacy and eroding public trust in government decision-making.

ve-1999.blurb: Venezuelan voters approved the new Bolivarian constitution in December 1999, consolidating executive power, weakening legislative and judicial independence, and providing the legal foundation for Chávez's "Bolivarian Revolution" — he remained in power until his death in 2013.

ve-2007.blurb: Chavez suffered his first electoral defeat when voters narrowly rejected his sweeping constitutional overhaul in December 2007, but he repackaged the centerpiece demand — abolition of presidential term limits — as a standalone amendment that Venezuelan voters ratified in February 2009, allowing him to seek re-election indefinitely.
